Okay, this interview with Tech Stevens July the 21st, 1995. This is real one. Okay, so I think we're... Okay. Let me just... Let me try to get this one here. Okay, first I want to ask you your birthday and your name.

June 10th, 1921. My name is George E. Stevens Jr. Everybody calls me Tex. That name stuck with me. I have relatives in Houston, Texas. And during the summer, I would go after school and after college some years into Houston where my relatives are. And I would come back with the big cowboy hat, being tall and wearing the hat. They started calling me Tex years ago. So they seem like they forgot about my first name. And the name just stuck. So I just started using it in business and everywhere I went. Even the various fraternities that I belong to. I just signed Tex Stevens and everybody worldwide know who I am. Because I belong to the Prince Hall Masonic Lodge, which is the largest black fraternal organization in the world. So that's how the name stuck. But all in all, I'm just enjoying life for these 74 years.
As a kid, I mean kids would call you that?

Well, around about 10, 12 years of age they started calling me that. Maybe a little later, around 12, 13 or something like that. That I was aware of it. Did you say you were born here in New Orleans? I was born in New Orleans.
And what street did you grow up on?

Where? Well, I lived on both sides of the river. First, I was born on Tex Street in Algiers on the west bank of the river. And then my mother moved to, well, we were living in Gretna on the west bank of the river. I was on 5th Street right across from Hebe's Old Bakery where my mother and father separated. Well, we moved over here into the Irish Channel, 515 Third Street. Well, incidentally, Ted, I went up that way about three or four months ago to look at the old house that I used to live in. But it's a warehouse district up there right now. Oh, okay, right here now. See, so things have changed tremendously. And I was lucky enough, I think about eight or ten years ago, to take a picture of the old house that I used to live in, the Irish Channel. That was one of the areas where a lot of politics came out of the Irish Channel also. Those were the good days. Then, while there, I attended to James Lewis School, which was on Annunciation Street at the time. And I really enjoyed that. I met a lot of friends. And incidentally, that was part of the old 10th Ward. And a lot of things have changed in that old 10th Ward area because they have a housing project there now. And a lot of the kids that I grew up with and the elders and whatnot, they're all gone. Or either they moved out of the way. And it's nothing but the housing development that's there right now. Just for the record, would you spell Stevens? S-T-E-P-H-E-N-S-I. Incidentally, I'm a junior. I'm named after my father.
Could you tell me something about your father and your father's family?
Well, my father...
When your parents were married, do you know anything about the family history in general?

Well, my father is from... He was from Macon, Georgia. I didn't know too much about my father's people. My father was a nomad. He was a barrel maker during the time that he married my mother. And he went to barbering school and he learned how to cut hair and things. What school I really don't know. See, my father died way back in 1970. But all in all, he lived to be around about 96... Between 95 and 96 years of age. My mother lived to be about 95. Incidentally, what I didn't mention... My mother was something like an accomplished pianist. And the first time I found out anything about jazz, my mother promoted the first night jazz concert on the West Bank of the River. To my knowledge, I was around about five, six years of age at that particular time. And I remember quite clearly all of the music woke me up. I went outside in my little undergarments, whatever I had on at the time. And boy, I listened to all of that doggone music. I said, wow, what a good time that was. And incidentally, that was... I'm trying to think. The guy was right down the street. My father had a barber shop with his sign out. The guy was in the same block with my father. And the band's gonna come to me, incidentally. I really enjoyed it. And somewhere in time, my mother would buy the old 78 records. And they had the old thing called a gramophone. What was it? In a player, you had to crank it up a couple of times. And you play it. It had the picture of the RCA dog on it and what not. And it just so happened that somewhere in time after my mother and father separated, I think my grandmother got angry and she put it out in the yard. It started raining and it ruined the doggone thing. That was a beautiful instrument.
So when you made the move from Test Street to 3rd?
515 3rd Street here in Orleans Parish.
When was that?

515 3rd Street. That was back in the 1930s, about 1935, 34, 35, something like that. And then I went to James Lewis School, which I said was up on Annunciation Street. Annunciation Street, somewhere up in that area. But they've moved to school since then.
What was your mother's maiden name?

Taylor. My mother's father was Lewis Taylor, who was a huntsman and a carpenter. And he was a pretty rough character. Lewis, they used to call him tits because he was a good man with his hands. You see tits, you hit your tit for tat and used to knock a lot of people out. That's what youngsters would fight with their hands, you know. My grandmother, I don't know too much about her because, you see, she died something. She went on to a grocery or something. And what happened was that on her way back home from what I understand, she fell into a well behind a church over in Gretton. She was drowned. I don't know whether it was raining that day or what happened. I really don't know what really happened to my grandmother. But that's the way it was told to me. And I was a very small child at that particular time. I think I was about maybe one or two years of age when all of this happened. But I had beautiful pictures of my grandmother. I still have them, but they're somewhere in my files. But God bless her soul.
And that concert you said your mother promoted, do you remember who the musicians were?

The leader of the band, I'll have to get back to that, it's on the tip of my hand, was a trumpet player. I'm trying to think of his name, it was on the tip of my tongue. It'll eventually come to me. It'll eventually come to me. He used to go to Europe every now and then because he passed on also. That was a very nice group. He's one of the old legendary Dixieland or blues type jazz trumpet players from way back. It's on the tip of my tongue. I'm thinking Oscar Celestine, Papa Celestine?
No,

He lived on the West Bank there for a while. He was a good friend of Mineta. He and Mineta were very, very good friends. That's another tremendous character, Mineta. He was from over in Algiers in the West Bank of the River. Did you know Mineta? I knew him slightly, but not personally as such. I'm trying to think of Clarence's name. Clarence and I went to Hoffman High School after I left the Mac down to 35. Clarence was a trumpet player who lived over in the Algiers. I'm trying to think of Clarence's last name. Tall, nice looking guy. Wore nice looking clothes all the time. But I think Clarence had a bad habit.
Uh-huh.

And I think he dropped out of school. And when I went into the Army somewhere in time, after living on both sides of the river, well, as I started growing up, I could come and go as I pleased at any given period of time because I still had a lot of relatives over on the West Bank, and I had a few relatives on this side of the river. Most of my relatives are immediate relatives. My mother's family was on the West Bank of the river, and some of her other cousins and aunts and whatnot, they were on this side of the river. Right. And I was in between both families from time to time.
As a kid, how would you cross the river?

Uh, we used to cross the old, these old ferry boat. Uh-huh. I didn't have an automobile incidental, that's the thing. It was about maybe, about three-quarters of a mile from my house on 5th Street in Greton. I crossed the ferry. And then, when I was going to Hoffman High School, I was walking about another two miles. I guess that's why I have pretty good legs today, because I did a lot of walking in my young life. Right. Lots of walking in my life.
And where would you catch the ferry to go?
I catch the ferry right there, Jackson Avenue.
Oh, okay. So it's that Jackson Avenue.

Yeah. Yeah, well, all that has changed. They reconstructed the buildings there. That's when they had the old, be so steam-like boat with the long pipe on top, with the crown, that looked like the king crown on the smokestack. Was it free to catch the ferry? Oh, it was free. Yeah. That's free to catch. That's free to catch. And then, sometimes, when I didn't, and as I got a little older, if I went to Algiers and hang out with some friends or whatever, and I wanted to come to New Orleans, you could also cross the Algiers ferry. That was free. They used to give you tickets. The Algiers used to give you tickets, but the Greton, if they saw you with school books, you could cross for free. But somewhere in time, they started giving you tickets, and I think I still had one or two of those tickets in my files somewhere. I'm something like a collector.
You're a back rat like me.
Just about.
You're a back rat.
Just about.
And were they segregated with all the ferry boats?

Yes. Let's face it. I am born on the other side of this thing called integration. I never had too much of a problem. I was well liked by a lot of whites. My mother, at one time, worked for the Hebe family. They were one of the richest families in Greton. They owned a big barber shop, and the oldest son became a lawyer, and he and I got to be very, very good friends. Bernard Hebe was his name, his name after his father, Mr. Bernard Hebe. They were very nice people, and like I said, when my mother and father separated, we were poor people. And we would just, whatever happened at that particular time, it just happened because you had no control over social issues when it came to becoming intermingling or shall we see associated with whites, the social posture and picture was all together a different kind of thing. You know, there was some certain complexity, complex, was a complex situation in a sense because whites wasn't particular about being socially enamored with blacks. But a lot of the whites were very nice people.
You said your mother worked for the Hebe's.
Worked for the Hebe's. What did she do? My mother did the housework for them since she was right across the street from them.
Was this her full-time job?
This was her full-time job after her and my father separated.
Did she work for any of the other families that she worked for?
At one time she worked for the Samuel family who owned one of the department stores over on Front Street in Gretna on the west bank of the river. And that was just about it.
So now you're on this side of the river mostly.

Well as I started growing. In the Irish Channel. Yeah well, see I lived in the Irish Channel for I think about three years and then we went back to Gretna. And that's how I happened to start walking after going to high school. See I graduated from Hoffman like around about 35, 36. Then I went to 1935 and I think I spent about a year and a half at Hoffman. Then I went to Macdonald 35 because I graduated from high school when I was 15 years of age.
Was Hoffman a junior high?

Yeah, junior high. Then you went to Macdonald 35. See at that time all you had was a school called Gaudet. You had Macdonald 35. Booker T. Washington hadn't been born then. You know. And we also had another school up here where LaSalle High School is. That was called.

not go at it, that was, it's going to eventually come to it, I just looked at the name here the other day, I'm just trying to think and talk with this microphone, I'm really at ease, but I'm just trying to recall so many different things in my life.
They'll come back to us and we can answer the question. Sure. So, specifically, was there anything in school you were terribly interested in, any subjects that you were on? Did you excel there?

Well, you see, my mother and father were not highly educated people, but even though my mother was a very good piano player, and she did domestic work on the side, but she learned how to play the piano because my father was paying the rate when they were living together, and after being separated, well, things started changing in the household. You see, then again, I think my Uncle William and them, they were some of the ones that was partly financing my mother. See, my Uncle William Thornton, he was a carpenter, but he had a sideline job. He used to sell stoop-down from the window. Stoop-down is liquor that they made in the bathtub, and they sold it to their various friends and whatnot. But it was a good proof, the way Grandma Phoebe said, it was a great proof that she lived to be about 105 years old, drinking the stuff, you know? So, all in all, William Thornton, well, he became his best customer somewhere in time, and he died with cirrhosis of the liver. He was around about 60-some years of age when he died. But all in all, you know, he bought him an automobile, bought him an old Ford automobile, at some time, that's when you could buy a new car for around about six, seven hundred dollars back in 1922, 23, 24, and 25. Or the high, when you paid over a thousand dollars for automobile, you were in the Cadillac class, just about. Of course, I don't remember it, I just saw the automobiles, and that was it.
So, as I can answer the question, were you very motivated in school?

In a sense, I was a good average student. I was always a good talking type of person. I could always rap pretty good, as you would say. My subjects were history. I wasn't a very good mathematician, not even today, but I liked math, but I never would take the time to concentrate on it. But I can do it pretty good now, after growing up working in business with it. But I was mostly into history, and geography, and technical things like that. And then, see, I learned how to swim in the Mississippi River. I remember, as I grew up, when I was about eleven years of age, they caught me swimming in the river. We couldn't afford a swimsuit. I had an old, cut-off pair of pants, but I lost them. And when I got out the water, this white police officer saw me, and I would stand up in the nude, and they put me in jail. In fact, they put all of us black guys in jail on the west back of the river. Well, the guy who a lot of people remember over there mostly was a guy by the name of B.H. Miller, B.R. Miller Sr., who was the chief of police at that particular time. Of course, I got along pretty good with B.H. because the house on Fifth Street was right across the street from the jailhouse. And whenever my father thought I was doing something bad, they would tell me, I'm going to have the police to come get you. Whenever I saw that automobile, I saw him with that big hat on, before I would run. I was scared of the police for a while. Until I started growing up and realized that as long as I wasn't doing anything, the man wasn't going to bother me.
What happened when the cops got you, picked you up from the-

Well, they locked me up over in the jail across the house, and so one of the officers went and got my mother. And that's when I found out what Amazing Grace was all about. My mother beat my behind from a can of tomato paste to Amazing Grace. That's when I found out what Amazing Grace was all about. Boy, did I hoop and holler that day. And I started being good after that. I think I have marks on the back of my rear end right now because, see, my mother had a cat of nine tails. I don't know if you ever saw anything like that. It was a strap with nine pieces of thin leather cut. And then my mother had a wire put into the tips. And I had marks on the back of my behind where she used to- I thought my mother hated me for a while. But as I grew somewhere in time, my mother really loved me. I realized what she was really doing as I grew. She was trying to make me become, I guess, the man that I am today to go to school, to go to college, and to do constructive things. My Jewish association is coming out with me. I'm going to talk with my hands, Ted. That happens sometime. I have a lot of Jewish friends also. So that's- So did you talk with your hands? Yeah. I got a little too close to the microphone.
Was your mother religious? And did you-

My mother was a Baptist. My father was a Baptist. My grandmother was a Baptist. The whole family was just about Baptist. But somewhere in time, my mother started leaning toward Catholicism. But she wouldn't go to church, but she had white friends who she would probably go play piano for at little sessions in their home. And she took a lot of, I guess those white people- By that time, I think I was about three or four years of age. I see mother come home with a couple of dollars every now and then. I was four or five years of age. That was before she had that jazz concert in the backyard where the party was jumping. But that was the story right then and then. She played for a few of the whites. It was very nice.
Do you think anything connected with the Hebe family?

Well, I think it was the Hebe family who knew that she was playing. She could play piano. They had white friends and they told her about my mother. But my mother was a little shy about getting involved with organized groups to play piano. She always wanted to do it by herself. So I don't know why. Because that was before my-

What type of music did your mother play? Well she played a combination of jazz and blues. She had a fast right hand. And she could pound that bass. I can just about hear her playing now. She wanted me to play piano. But I don't know, I didn't have an interest in it. In fact she bought a piano for me to play. And there was a lady who played in the regular Baptist church where most of my family were members.

And she was living on the same time. And she was living on this side of the river. And I took a couple of lessons from her. But when my mother found out I wasn't interested, she just beat the hell out of me. And she stopped paying for it. And that was the add to that. Because I was mostly interested in history and swimming, baseball, and football. I was a good athlete. But then again, who was looking at me 65, 70 years ago. Because I was a very good first baseman. I played on championship teams. Well who did you play baseball for? The Algiers Giants. And I played for the Gretton All-Stars.
Now the Algiers, okay, you have to back up. What was this?

It was Sandlot Baseball. Was it organized in any way? Well it was semi-organized. Because first I started playing with the Gretton All-Stars. It was a fellow by the name of Wesley Barrow who later became general manager of the Baltimore Eli Giants back in the 50s. And Wesley Barrow came out of Franklin, Louisiana. But he was a hefty man. But he had something like a YMCA, a USO, or whatever you want to call it. He always kept young people together. People like J.B. Spencer who also went to the Homestead Grays. And also to a couple of other black professional baseball teams at that particular time. He and Herbert Simpson, George McDay. I can call the name of a lot of baseball players. Right from the Dretton area, from the Algiers area, from the Hammond area. And all like that. Because we all played together. We had to play together. Because whites wouldn't play together. Now I'll tell you what really happened. Mel Ott, who was from over in Grettona. Mel Ott, and Buddy Beeson, who was a shortstop. I can't think of Buddy's name. We just called him Buddy Beeson. Now he and Mel Ott, Wesley Barrow, and Chester Stamps, they all used to work out in an empty lot way back on the far side of Grettona about 75 years ago. I can remember that because I used to stand on the sideline trying to wait to learn how to play the game, what it was all about at that time. I was about five or six years of age. But I remember that very clearly. Now Mel Ott and several other white baseball players, but they wouldn't play as a team as such. But they used to work out and practice together. That's what they did. So, uh... I had a fellow over there by the name of Mookow Miller, who his family owned something like a milk farm over there in Grettona. And he was a tremendous pitcher. They used to call him Mookow Miller. I think where they used to sell the milk from up on Fifth Street, I think that old building is still there. I think it's a historical document. It's one of these good days. I think somebody's going to take a picture of it if they haven't done it already.
Now what were the professional black teams that played in this area? What did New Orleans have the professional black teams?

Well, you had the New Orleans black pelicans named after the New Orleans white baseball team. Then you had the Morris Moore All-Stars. Then you had the Jacks Red Sox. You had quite a few. You had a fellow by the name of Robinson. I'm trying to think of Robinson, who was one of the so-called big-time chefs from New Orleans, who was a professional restaurant. I was a restaurant tour who went to New York and opened a big-time restaurant. I'm trying to think of Robinson's first name. In fact, he sent me a letter sometime before he died. He was managing one of the baseball teams in and around the New Orleans Jefferson-Pierre area. Then they had the Winfield Devils. I played with them the first time I had an official suit. It was a blood red suit trimmed with black. A fellow by the name of Winfield over in Algiers. He was the owner of that baseball team. The reason why I'm putting this together, Ted, we did not have a lot of crime at that time. Very few blacks owned pistols now. Some of us family fathers or grandfathers owned shotguns. You've got to remember, Gretna and New Orleans was not highly developed at that time. You could go hunting. You could go hunting in those particular areas. It was the only guns that I remember seeing at that time in history. But there wasn't any crime of no crime. Well, people would get killed. It was mostly domestic things, to my knowledge. Now and then, you would hear talk of somebody. But as far as blacks holding up each other, killing, when you go back 65, 70 years now, rarely did you hear of anything like that. Because, you see, Gretna was what you would call old Gretna Greens, named after some particular geographical area over in England. And it was a very small, small community. And Gretna didn't have paved streets until somewhere around about the mid-1930s. Because everything was dirt. Dirt streets and roads at that time. And, you know, very few people had automobiles. The ones, which was only the wealthy people, very few blacks had automobiles at that time, to my knowledge. The Johnson family, one of the black families over in Gretna, they were the first black family, other than my Uncle William, to own an automobile.
So that was it. Where, where, where, where the black, uh, professional games, where were they played? What were the first games?

Most of the games, most of the games were played, uh, even, uh, in Gretna, or even Algiers on this side of the river, uh, in, uh, the various parks on this side of the river, in Gretna. I'm trying to think of the name of the dog, on the park up there. Uh, sometime they would, uh, play down in Houma. Sometime the, the various teams would, uh, uh, would go out of town, uh, uh, to play.
Was there, was there a park in McDonaville?

There was a park in McDonaville also. There was a park in Algiers. And you had about two or three parks. You had a park up in Califant. I'm trying to think of the name of it right now. Then you had a park, uh, a park down in the Ninth Ward out near.

one of the, let's see, in the Gentile area, I can't think of the name of all of these things. You're coming at me so fast, Ted, I'm trying to reach back in my memory as to what was going on at that time in history, but you had some tremendous baseball players to come out of New Orleans, like Herman Ross, J.B. Spencer, Wesley Barrow, you know, I could just name a lot of people, Squatty Benjamin, I'm just trying to think of some of the guys.
These went on to play pro, though.

Yeah, most of them, semi-pro or either pro baseball, they played with the Homestead Grays, or either they played with the Monarchs, or either they played with other black football, baseball teams. And incidentally, New Orleans was the first city to have an organized semi-pro football team also.
When was the assistant?

This was in the 40s and into the 50s. You know, New Orleans had, beside being noted number one for jazz and blues and whatnot. We were first in a lot of things, in sports and things Now you're talking about baseball, I always see the photo of Louis Armstrong with his
baseball team, Armstrong Secret Nine.

Yeah, he financed that team. Did you know any of the players in that? No, I didn't. I did not know any of the players. Because I've always looked at that photograph and I'm wondering who those players are, where of the Zulu club.
No, it could have been, maybe that was before my time. See, I've been around the Zulu since 1949, I wasn't an official member of the Zulu club.

I was an escort for Louis Armstrong in 1949 when he was a king because I drove one of the automobiles for him and I was an escort for his wife also. And I tell you, those were the good old days but not about the baseball players for the Zulu club. See, I was an honor, I remember I just started paying dues around about, I guess about 25, 30 years ago or something like that when I left town and came back and they needed money. And see what they did, the Zulus used to beg for money in the community from various businesses of friends and most of their white friends and a few blacks. But today, the Zulu organization is a worldwide international organization. They support themselves. We have doctors, lawyers, professional people like myself, engineers, technicians, and then we are integrated. We have about 10 or 12 of them. I want to tape some of that. I should have brought some with me. The next time we get together, maybe between now and Saddare, either one day next week, I'll bring some of them and I'll

play them and let you listen to them. Yeah, if you want to do that. So, we're on reel number two with Tex Stevens. It's still July the 21st, 1995. July the 1st. Yeah, we're talking about we're talking about, yeah, pro baseball and sports in general. Yeah, and I didn't realize how much

had come out of this area, how much sports. Well, we had a lot of sports and stuff that came out of this area. But then again, you have to thank people like, like, Jack Moore and a few other people, Champ Clark. Then you had people like, Wendy, New Orleans Recreation Department, Jeff was put together. Jeff, Jeff, Jeff, Morris, I think, Jeff was the first black to get involved. Morris, Jeff was a graduate of Zive University and also Chicago University. And he opened many doors for young kids to come out. And they started naming playgrounds. When Mayor Morrison became, became mayor for the city of New Orleans, things were beginning to change. You would begin to see a little gap in the social patterns between blacks and whites. There was a new development. The human equation was beginning to spell itself for the structure of Americanism to become a composite force where the chemistry was beginning to showcase itself because Mayor Morrison and the city council, they were beginning to recognize a few people who were politically like Reverend A. Lincoln Davis and a few other people who were in the political structure at that time. Why do you think that was happening at that time? You're talking, I mean, Morrison comes into office in 1948. Well, let me tell you how it all started. It started. It started with Huey Long, who had that theme, every man a king and a chicken in every pot. And Long opened the door for a lot of blacks to get registered. And then the local politicians were beginning to take a look at the black population growing. And then the schools were beginning to open up. Blacks were beginning to get educated, just like I showed you this thing with my great-grandfather. I was on that committee in 1909 when McKinley came to New Orleans. And there was a new focus into the lifestyle of blacks. Whites were beginning to come into the community to ask blacks to vote for them. And this was beginning to have a new challenge for the political atmosphere for New Orleans. And you had people like Ernest Wright, who started one of the first registration campaigns in the city of New Orleans. And these people were beginning to really develop a new type of image factor for the political structure in the city of New Orleans and the state of Louisiana. Earl Amity, who was a high school classmate of mine, who was a tremendous lawyer, who became one of the attorneys on the staff of John Dowling. Not John Dowling, Mr. Dowling, John's uncle, his uncle or his brother, was a district attorney. Earl Amity, I can remember very clearly because I was on the radio in 1955, 56 or something like that. And I just got angry and I started berating the community, talking down about white people and so forth and so on. So somebody called Dowling, that district attorney's office and they wanted to know who was that nigger on the radio on old WMRY before it was WYLD. Raising all that hell and talking down about the white citizen council and all this kind of stuff. So, somehow or another Dowling opened his office at City Hall on a Sunday and I had to get Earl Amity to represent me. So Earl and I went down there and he and Dowling got to be the very best of friends. That was about 52, 53 or something like that. I'll never forget that law because I was kind of scared there for a while. I said district attorney wanted me.
Well, what were they going to charge you with? I mean, what could they have?

Well, I don't know what he was charging me, but they, but a certain, certain whites and I got, got it in black and white. I got letters and I have cards that were sent to me by the white citizen council. And, uh, incidentally, uh, prior to that, I was a registered Republican incidentally, and I was on a Republican committee, uh, when, uh, when, uh, um, Eisenhower was running for office. And I sold somewhere around about, uh, a few hundred dollars worth of tickets. They wouldn't even let me go into the front door to attend the affair when Eisenhower came to New Orleans at Fairmount Hotel. Today I can walk in the door and incidentally today, I also handled some of the advertising for the Fairmount Hotel as the account executive for the Fairmount. I did it for a while. And, uh, so things were beginning to change. And, uh, I, I'll say great day for the city of New Orleans. There were some beautiful things were beginning to happen. And I guess I can tell some, uh, dynamic stories about people who, uh, accelerated, uh, the new ideology. Uh, in the city of New Orleans, Jackson V. A Cox, uh, the state representative Avery Alexander, Carl Gallman. Uh, maybe a lot of people may not like some of these names I'm calling, but these people, uh, they, they agitated the situation. Well, you know what an agitator is. You throw your clothes in the washing machine. An agitator with the soap will get the clean, will get your clothes clean. This is what agitator is all about. But it was a lot of fun. But, uh, they didn't lock me up when I went before Dallin. But, uh, Dallin and I, Mr. Dallin and I got to be very, very good friends. segments.chapter: Opening and childhood on the West Bank
segments.title: Opening of the interview and recording details
segments.summary: Tex Stephens settles in; the interviewer announces the date, July 21, 1995, and asks his name and birthday.

segments.chapter: Opening and childhood on the West Bank
segments.title: Birthdate and how George Stephens became 'Tex'
segments.summary: Born June 10, 1921, he explains the nickname came from cowboy hats brought back from relatives in Houston, and that it stuck in business and fraternities.

segments.chapter: Opening and childhood on the West Bank
segments.title: Growing up in Algiers, Gretna and the Irish Channel
segments.summary: He lists the homes he lived in on both sides of the river, from Algiers and Gretna to 515 Third Street in the Irish Channel, and James Lewis School.

segments.chapter: Opening and childhood on the West Bank
segments.title: His father the barber, and his mother's first jazz concert
segments.summary: He describes his father from Macon and his mother the pianist, who promoted a night jazz concert on the West Bank when he was five or six, and the gramophone ruined in the rain.

segments.chapter: Opening and childhood on the West Bank
segments.title: Maternal grandparents, Lewis Taylor and the drowned grandmother
segments.summary: His mother's maiden name was Taylor; he tells of his rough carpenter grandfather and how his grandmother drowned in a well.

segments.chapter: Opening and childhood on the West Bank
segments.title: Who played the concert: a trumpet leader and Algiers friends
segments.summary: Tex tries to recall the trumpet player who led the band at his mother's concert, and mentions Mineta and a trumpeter classmate named Clarence from Algiers.

segments.chapter: Opening and childhood on the West Bank
segments.title: Crossing the river by ferry between two families
segments.summary: He moved between relatives on both banks and crossed on the free Jackson Avenue ferry, walking to Hoffman school.

segments.chapter: Opening and childhood on the West Bank
segments.title: Segregation, the Hebe family and his mother's housework
segments.summary: He discusses segregated ferries and relations with whites, and how his mother did housework for the Hebe and Samuel families after his parents separated.

segments.chapter: Opening and childhood on the West Bank
segments.title: Hoffman and McDonogh 35 schooling
segments.summary: He recounts living in the Irish Channel then returning to Gretna, finishing Hoffman junior high and going on to McDonogh 35 at age 15.

segments.chapter: Opening and childhood on the West Bank
segments.title: Parents' limited education and Uncle William's liquor
segments.summary: Asked about school interests, Tex describes his parents' modest means and Uncle William Thornton, a carpenter who sold homemade liquor and died of cirrhosis.

segments.chapter: Opening and childhood on the West Bank
segments.title: Swimming in the river, jail and his mother's whipping
segments.summary: He was a history-loving student who learned to swim in the Mississippi, was jailed at eleven with other boys, and was beaten by his mother.

segments.chapter: Opening and childhood on the West Bank
segments.title: Mother's religion and her jazz and blues piano
segments.summary: His family was Baptist; his mother played piano for white friends and played fast jazz and blues, and wanted her son to play.

segments.chapter: Sandlot baseball and New Orleans sports
segments.title: Piano lessons abandoned for sandlot baseball
segments.summary: He took a few piano lessons but preferred sports, playing first base for the Algiers Giants and the Gretna All-Stars under Wesley Barrow.

segments.chapter: Sandlot baseball and New Orleans sports
segments.title: Black professional teams, parks and life in Gretna
segments.summary: He names New Orleans black teams like the Black Pelicans and Winfield Devils, describes Gretna's dirt streets and few guns, and the parks games were played in.

segments.chapter: Sandlot baseball and New Orleans sports
segments.title: Local ballplayers who went pro and New Orleans sports firsts
segments.summary: He names players who went to the Homestead Grays and Monarchs, and says New Orleans had the first organized semi-pro football team.

segments.chapter: Sandlot baseball and New Orleans sports
segments.title: Armstrong's Secret Nine and escorting Louis Armstrong as Zulu king, 1949
segments.summary: Asked about Armstrong's baseball team, Tex says he did not know the players but drove for Armstrong as Zulu king in 1949, and describes the Zulu club's growth.

segments.chapter: Politics and Jonestown
segments.title: Recreation leaders, Mayor Morrison and changing politics
segments.summary: After a reel change, Tex credits Jack Moore, Morris Jeff and Huey Long with opening doors, describes Morrison-era political change, and his 1950s radio run-in with the district attorney.

segments.chapter: Politics and Jonestown
segments.title: White Citizens Council, Eisenhower tickets and an integrated political group
segments.summary: He tells of the DA affair, being refused entry at an Eisenhower event, and forming a New Orleans political association with Earl Amadee and others.

segments.chapter: Politics and Jonestown
segments.title: Taft reception brochure and the Jonestown Wolves Club
segments.summary: He shows a brochure from his grandfather Lewis Taylor's files about the Taft reception, and begins describing Jonestown's marching Wolves Club.

segments.chapter: Politics and Jonestown
segments.title: Wolves Hall, West Bank lounges and parades
segments.summary: He describes the Wolves Hall and cousins who ran West Bank lounges that hosted Fats Domino and Tommy Ridgley, and how the Wolves marched on holidays.

segments.chapter: Politics and Jonestown
segments.title: Father's barbershop and the Brotherhood Eyes gossip sheet
segments.summary: His father's Gretna barbershop drew men from Sam Peet's ballroom, and Tex recalls the gossip paper Brotherhood Eyes.

segments.chapter: Irish Channel youth, newspapers and McDonogh 35
segments.title: Mardi Gras and the Irish Channel street gang
segments.summary: He recalls watching parades, masking, and fighting in a neighborhood gang with Jonas Monroe, plus the mostly white bands he heard at Carnival.

segments.chapter: Irish Channel youth, newspapers and McDonogh 35
segments.title: Selling newspapers as a boy
segments.summary: At ten or eleven he sold the Item for a penny on Washington Avenue, later the Louisiana Weekly, earning pennies for rent of a dollar a month.

segments.chapter: Irish Channel youth, newspapers and McDonogh 35
segments.title: McDonogh 35 graduation and Rampart Street neighbors
segments.summary: He graduated in 1937 from McDonogh 35 on Rampart Street, near Shaiky's Crazy House and the Chinese restaurant of Harry Lee's family.

segments.chapter: Irish Channel youth, newspapers and McDonogh 35
segments.title: McDonogh 35 classmates and Thelma Brown
segments.summary: He lists schoolmates and relatives who graduated from McDonogh 35, and remembers his sweetheart Thelma Brown.

segments.chapter: Irish Channel youth, newspapers and McDonogh 35
segments.title: High school hangouts and working for tailor Lewis Silvers
segments.summary: He went to Rampart Street and West Bank clubs, and Lewis Silvers the tailor gave him his first zoot suit, a job and money for Xavier.

segments.chapter: After high school: riverfront and tailoring
segments.title: After high school: riverfront sack sewing and Xavier
segments.summary: At fifteen he considered medical school or athletics, worked on the riverfront sewing sacks, and saved money to attend Xavier for nearly two years.

segments.chapter: After high school: riverfront and tailoring
segments.title: Meeting Lewis Silvers and the meaning of the zoot suit
segments.summary: A salesman named Warren brought him to Silvers' shop; Tex explains the zoot suit style tied to Cab Calloway and Count Basie.

segments.chapter: After high school: riverfront and tailoring
segments.title: Palace Theater big bands and the Natchez fire
segments.summary: He and friends heard big bands at the Palace Theater and Tick Tock, and he tells how a lack of money kept them from a Natchez show that burned.

segments.chapter: After high school: riverfront and tailoring
segments.title: Rampart Street as the Black main street and its tailor shops
segments.summary: He describes Rampart, Dryades and Dryad Streets as the Black business area, the tailor shops, suit prices then and now, and shopping in Dallas.

segments.chapter: Rampart Street night life
segments.title: A walking tour of Rampart Street clubs, Roy Brown and radio
segments.summary: Block by block he names clubs from the Pelican to the Downbeat, Roy Brown, B.B. King at the Blue Eagle, Haze's, disc jockeys, and Army nights in Washington.

segments.chapter: Rampart Street night life
segments.title: Iceberg Slim and the pimps he knew in Washington
segments.summary: He recalls meeting a golden-tongued pimp called Iceberg Slim in Washington, D.C., and the polite terms for prostitutes.

segments.chapter: Rampart Street night life
segments.title: New Orleans pimps, and the uptown clubs and big band halls
segments.summary: He says New Orleans pimps trained those in Houston and New York, names local pimps, then lists clubs such as the Dew Drop, Robin Hood and the Pythian Temple.

segments.chapter: Rampart Street night life
segments.title: The Pythian Temple and his father's lodge
segments.summary: Asked about dances at the Pythian, he says he was too young but his father belonged to the Knights of Pythias and Odd Fellows.

segments.chapter: Radio, records and history
segments.title: Hearing Louis Armstrong on the radio in the 1930s
segments.summary: He did not see Armstrong at the Astoria in 1936 but heard him on the radio from the whites-only Suburban club.

segments.chapter: Radio, records and history
segments.title: No radio at home and his mother's few records
segments.summary: His family could not afford a radio; he first heard one at a neighbor's, and his mother had a few old records.

segments.chapter: Radio, records and history
segments.title: Donating records to the jazz archives and why history matters
segments.summary: He began collecting records as a disc jockey, is donating 78s and photographs to the archive, and reflects on the value of recorded history.

segments.chapter: Silvers, Rampart Street and Army service
segments.title: Working for Mr. Silvers and learning Yiddish words
segments.summary: He worked on and off for Silvers for several years and picked up Yiddish phrases from the shop, and Charles Talford, his indirect boss.

segments.chapter: Silvers, Rampart Street and Army service
segments.title: Charles Talford and Dave Brown, mayor of Rampart Street
segments.summary: He identifies Talford as a big well-dressed Rampart presence and Dave Brown, whose all-night Keyhole featured Professor Longhair and Smiley Lewis.

segments.chapter: Silvers, Rampart Street and Army service
segments.title: The extent of his Yiddish
segments.summary: He can follow Jewish conversations and food terms like gefilte but cannot speak the language.

segments.chapter: Silvers, Rampart Street and Army service
segments.title: Drafted in 1942 and kept in the States by special services
segments.summary: Drafted into the 92nd Division infantry at Fort McClellan, he trained soldiers and, because he could read a map, was kept from combat in special services.

segments.chapter: Silvers, Rampart Street and Army service
segments.title: Army newspaper writing and first radio appearance
segments.summary: He wrote for the company newspaper and once introduced a gospel group on Washington radio, then reflects on learning from mistakes.

segments.chapter: Silvers, Rampart Street and Army service
segments.title: Studying at Xavier before the Army
segments.summary: He spent almost two years at Xavier in general courses toward medicine, drawn away by thoughts of the Army, girls and his sick mother.

segments.chapter: Silvers, Rampart Street and Army service
segments.title: Parents, segregation, the bank dispute and WWL
segments.summary: He talks about his father's many children, segregation limiting his parents, a bank he took his money from, an honorary doctorate and being turned down at WWL.

segments.chapter: Postwar career and reflections
segments.title: Cosmo Matassa and documenting history while living
segments.summary: The interviewer relays Cosmo's remarks about being too busy making a living for history; Tex stresses documenting history and not wasting time.

segments.chapter: Postwar career and reflections
segments.title: After the war: riverfront, Informer Sentinel column and Black clubs
segments.summary: Back from service he worked the riverfront, then John Russo and Elgin Hychew got him writing a column, covering clubs while Black patrons could not go to the French Quarter.

segments.chapter: Postwar career and reflections
segments.title: French Quarter segregation, Fats Pichon, Ronnie Kole and education
segments.summary: He tells of first entering French Quarter clubs, Fats Pichon at the Absinthe House, Ronnie Kole, Earl Williams barred from the bar, and the need for education.
